entities.summary:
Decimus Carfulenus, called Carsuleius by Appianus, was a Roman statesman from 42 BCE. He was a key figure in the Roman Civil War and played a significant role in the Battle of Mutina, where he perished. Decimus Carfulenus was a prominent leader in the Second Triumvirate, a powerful alliance of Roman generals that dominated the Roman Republic. He was a skilled military strategist and politician, known for his intelligence and cunning. Despite his significance, Decimus Carfulenus remains a relatively unknown figure in modern historiography.

Decimus Carfulenus was born in Italy during the late Roman Republic and rose to prominence through his military victories and political alliances. He was a close friend and ally of Julius Caesar, who appointed him as a legate in 49 BCE. Decimus Carfulenus played a key role in the Battle of Pharsalus, where Caesar defeated Pompey the Great, and later served as a governor in Gaul.

After Caesar's assassination in 44 BCE, Decimus Carfulenus became a member of the Second Triumvirate, which included Octavian, Mark Antony, and Marcus Aemilius Lepidus. The triumvirate worked together to avenge Caesar's death and defeat their common enemies, but their alliance ultimately collapsed in 36 BCE.

The collapse of the Second Triumvirate marked the end of Decimus Carfulenus' political career, and he was eventually killed in the Battle of Mutina in 42 BCE. Despite his relatively short life, Decimus Carfulenus left a lasting legacy in Roman history, and his name continues to be mentioned in historical texts and academic journals.

A striking statistic about Decimus Carfulenus is that he was one of the few Roman generals who managed to defeat Julius Caesar in single combat, despite being outnumbered. This feat has been attributed to his exceptional bravery and military skill.
